title: Sound Foundations & Low-End Physics
description: A foundation module that explains what sound physically is, how waves move through air, why low frequencies behave differently from higher frequencies, and how wavelength, amplitude, phase, and room boundaries shape what we hear.

lessons.title: What Sound Actually Is
lessons.body:
Sound begins with motion. When an object vibrates, it pushes and pulls on the particles around it. In air, those tiny changes create alternating regions of slightly higher and lower pressure that travel outward from the source.
The air itself does not travel from the loudspeaker to your ear. Individual air molecules mostly move back and forth around their resting positions. What travels through the room is the disturbance — a repeating pattern of compression and rarefaction carrying energy from one place to another.
This is why sound needs a medium. It can travel through gases, liquids, and solids because all of them contain particles that can transfer mechanical energy to neighboring particles. In a vacuum there is no material available to carry those pressure changes, so ordinary sound cannot propagate.
A loudspeaker demonstrates this clearly. When its diaphragm moves forward, it compresses nearby air. When it moves backward, it creates a region of lower pressure. If this motion repeats 100 times every second, the pressure pattern has a frequency of 100 Hz.
Our ears detect these pressure variations. The eardrum moves in response, the middle and inner ear convert that motion into neural signals, and the brain interprets those signals as pitch, loudness, timbre, location, and other characteristics.
Key relationship
Sound = mechanical vibration + medium + energy transfer
The source creates the vibration, the medium carries it, and the listener or microphone detects it.
Practical example
Place your hand near a loudspeaker playing a strong low-frequency tone. You may feel the movement of air and sometimes the vibration of nearby surfaces. These are physical effects of the same pressure changes that your ears interpret as sound.
Take away
 Sound is a mechanical pressure disturbance.
 Air particles oscillate locally rather than travelling with the sound.
 Sound requires a material medium to propagate.
 A microphone and an ear both respond to changing pressure.

lessons.title: Frequency, Period and Pitch
lessons.body:
Frequency describes how many complete cycles of a repeating vibration occur every second. It is measured in hertz, written as Hz. A 50 Hz signal completes 50 cycles each second, while a 1,000 Hz signal completes 1,000.
In simple periodic sounds, frequency is strongly related to perceived pitch. Lower frequencies are generally heard as lower pitches, while higher frequencies are heard as higher pitches. However, pitch is a perceptual quality rather than a direct measurement, so complex sounds can create more complicated pitch sensations.
The inverse of frequency is period. Period tells us how long one complete cycle takes.
Formula
T = 1 / f
Where:
T = period in seconds
f = frequency in hertz
For a 100 Hz signal:
T = 1 / 100 = 0.01 s = 10 ms
For a 50 Hz signal:
T = 1 / 50 = 0.02 s = 20 ms
This relationship becomes useful when working with oscillators, delay times, phase alignment, audio editing, and signal processing. A lower-frequency waveform takes more time to complete each cycle.
The audible range of a healthy young listener is often described approximately as 20 Hz to 20 kHz, although real hearing varies with age, listening level, and individual physiology. The lowest part of this range is especially interesting because very low frequencies may be experienced partly as physical vibration rather than only as tonal sound.
Practical example
A 40 Hz bass tone completes one cycle every:
T = 1 / 40 = 0.025 s = 25 ms
That means a single low-frequency cycle lasts much longer than one cycle of a 4 kHz tone, which lasts only:
T = 1 / 4000 = 0.00025 s = 0.25 ms
Take away
 Frequency tells you how many cycles occur each second.
 Hertz means cycles per second.
 Period tells you how long one cycle lasts.

lessons.title: Why Low Frequencies Have Long Wavelengths
lessons.body:
Frequency and wavelength are directly connected through the speed of sound. At typical room temperature, sound travels through air at roughly 343 metres per second.
If frequency decreases while the speed of sound stays approximately constant, the wavelength must increase.
Formula
λ = c / f
Where:
λ = wavelength in metres
c = speed of sound, approximately 343 m/s
f = frequency in Hz
For 40 Hz:
λ = 343 / 40 ≈ 8.58 m
For 60 Hz:
λ = 343 / 60 ≈ 5.72 m
For 100 Hz:
λ = 343 / 100 ≈ 3.43 m
These distances are large compared with the dimensions of many rooms. A bedroom might only be 4 or 5 metres long, meaning a 40 Hz wavelength can be considerably longer than the room itself.
That changes the way low frequencies interact with boundaries. Instead of behaving like narrow rays that can easily be aimed in a particular direction, bass frequencies tend to spread broadly and strongly excite the pressure field of the room.
Long wavelengths also explain why small physical adjustments can create large audible differences. Moving a subwoofer, changing the listening position, or adding another bass source can significantly alter how low-frequency energy combines inside the space.
At higher frequencies, wavelengths become much shorter. A 4 kHz sound has a wavelength of only about:
λ = 343 / 4000 ≈ 0.086 m
That is roughly 8.6 cm, which allows objects, surfaces, and even the human head to influence propagation much more strongly.
Practical example
Compare 50 Hz and 5 kHz:
50 Hz → λ ≈ 6.86 m
5 kHz → λ ≈ 0.069 m
The low-frequency wave is almost one hundred times longer. That difference helps explain why bass and treble behave so differently in a room.
Take away
 Lower frequency means longer wavelength.
 Bass wavelengths are often comparable to or larger than room dimensions.

lessons.title: Why Low End Is Nearly Omnidirectional
lessons.body:
Low-frequency sound is difficult to aim because its wavelength is large relative to most loudspeakers, furniture, and objects in a typical room.
When an object is much smaller than a wavelength, that object does not create a strong acoustic shadow. The wave tends to bend and spread around it rather than being cleanly blocked.
This is one reason subwoofers can often be placed without pointing them directly toward the listener. At very low frequencies, the radiation pattern is usually much less directional than the radiation of a high-frequency driver.
For example, a 40 Hz wavelength is approximately:
λ = 343 / 40 ≈ 8.6 m
Very few domestic loudspeakers or pieces of furniture are remotely comparable to that size. The wave therefore interacts with the entire room rather than travelling as a tightly controlled beam.
However, saying that bass is omnidirectional does not mean subwoofer placement is irrelevant. Placement strongly affects how the source interacts with walls, corners, floor boundaries, and room modes.
A subwoofer moved from the centre of a room toward a wall may produce a noticeably different frequency response. Moving it into a corner can increase low-frequency output because several boundaries reinforce the pressure field.
Listeners also experience positional effects. At one seat, two reflections may combine constructively and make a frequency very loud. A short distance away, the same frequency may partially cancel.
So low-frequency reproduction is better understood as pressure management throughout the room rather than simply aiming a speaker toward the listener.
Practical example
If a listener hears too little 50 Hz energy, rotating the subwoofer a few degrees may make almost no difference. Moving the subwoofer or the listening position by one metre may produce a dramatic change.
Take away
 Long wavelengths make bass difficult to aim.
 Low frequencies bend around relatively small obstacles.
 Subwoofer orientation matters less than placement at very low frequencies.
 Room boundaries strongly influence bass level.
 Listening position can change bass response dramatically.

lessons.title: Amplitude, Level and Decibels
lessons.body:
Amplitude describes the magnitude of a vibration or signal. In an acoustic wave, greater pressure variation generally corresponds to a stronger physical sound signal.
But audio level is rarely expressed using simple linear numbers. Instead, audio commonly uses the decibel, abbreviated dB.
The decibel is logarithmic. This is useful because both acoustic pressure and human hearing operate across extremely large ranges. A logarithmic scale compresses those ranges into manageable numbers.
For amplitude-related quantities, the relationship is commonly written as:
Formula
ΔdB = 20 log10(A2 / A1)
Where:
A1 = reference amplitude
A2 = new amplitude
If amplitude doubles:
20 log10(2) ≈ 6.02 dB
So doubling signal amplitude corresponds to approximately +6 dB.
For power quantities, a different relationship is used:
ΔdB = 10 log10(P2 / P1)
Doubling power gives:
10 log10(2) ≈ 3.01 dB
This distinction matters. Doubling electrical power is not the same mathematical operation as doubling signal amplitude.
Another important term is sound pressure level, or SPL. SPL compares measured acoustic pressure with a reference pressure and expresses the result in dB SPL.
A higher dB value means a larger physical level, but perceived loudness does not increase in a simple linear way. Human hearing sensitivity also changes with frequency, so two tones with the same measured SPL may not sound equally loud.
This is particularly relevant to bass. At moderate listening levels, very low frequencies often need greater physical SPL than midrange frequencies to produce a similar subjective sense of loudness.
Practical example
Suppose an audio signal changes from an amplitude of 0.25 to 0.50:
20 log10(0.50 / 0.25)
= 20 log10(2)
≈ +6.02 dB
The amplitude doubled, so the level increased by approximately 6 dB.
Take away
 Decibels express ratios on a logarithmic scale.
 Doubling amplitude gives approximately +6 dB.
 Doubling power gives approximately +3 dB.

lessons.title: Phase, Interference and Cancellation
lessons.body:
When two sound waves reach the same location, their instantaneous pressure values combine. This process is called superposition.
If the waves reinforce each other, the result is constructive interference. If they oppose each other, the result is destructive interference.
Phase describes the position of one periodic waveform relative to another waveform of the same frequency. It is commonly expressed in degrees.
A complete cycle contains:
360°
Two identical sine waves aligned at:
0° phase difference
will reinforce each other.
Two equal sine waves separated by:
180° phase difference
have opposite polarity at every point in the cycle and can theoretically cancel completely.
Real acoustic environments are more complicated because reflected waves travel different distances before reaching the listener. Those path differences create frequency-dependent phase shifts.
This means one reflection might reinforce 60 Hz while partially cancelling 90 Hz. The same room can therefore contain peaks and nulls at different frequencies.
Distance can also be expressed in terms of phase.
A path difference equal to one full wavelength corresponds to:
360°
Half a wavelength corresponds to:
180°
At 100 Hz, wavelength is approximately:
3.43 m
Half a wavelength is approximately:
1.715 m
If two equal 100 Hz signals arrive with a path-length difference close to 1.715 m, they may arrive roughly 180° apart and strongly cancel.
This is why adding another subwoofer does not automatically create better bass. The timing, distance, level, placement, and phase relationship between the sources determine whether they reinforce or cancel at a particular listening location.
Modern systems may use adjustable delay or phase controls to improve alignment. The goal is not simply to make every waveform visually identical but to create useful acoustic summation across the listening area.
Formula
Phase shift = 360° × Δd / λ
Where:
Δd = path-length difference
λ = wavelength
If a 100 Hz wave has a wavelength of 3.43 m and the path difference is 0.8575 m:
Phase shift = 360° × 0.8575 / 3.43 ≈ 90°
Practical example
Two subwoofers reproduce the same 80 Hz tone.
At one listening position, their waves arrive nearly in phase and the bass becomes stronger. At another position, the difference in path length causes the waves to arrive closer to opposite phase, producing a deep reduction in level.
Nothing is necessarily wrong with either subwoofer. The difference comes from the way their waves combine in space.
Take away
 Sound waves combine through superposition.
 In-phase signals reinforce each other.
 Opposite-phase signals can produce strong cancellation.
 Path length creates phase differences.
 Phase behaviour changes with frequency.
 Multiple bass sources must be aligned and positioned carefully.

title: Room Acoustics & Bass Behavior
description: This module explains what happens when sound leaves the speaker and enters a real room. It focuses on reflections, standing waves, room modes, boundary reinforcement, listening position, and the practical reasons bass response can change dramatically from one part of a room to another.

lessons.title: What Happens When Sound Hits a Room
lessons.body:
A room is not a passive container for sound. The moment a loudspeaker begins to play, sound travels toward every nearby surface — walls, floor, ceiling, furniture, windows, and other objects.
When a sound wave reaches a boundary, several things may happen at the same time.
Part of the energy may be reflected back into the room.
 Part may be absorbed by the material.
 Part may pass through the structure as transmitted energy.
 Part may be scattered in different directions.
The balance between these processes depends strongly on frequency.
A thick soft material may absorb a significant amount of high-frequency energy but do very little at low frequencies. Bass wavelengths are long, which makes them much harder to absorb effectively with thin materials.
This means a room can behave very differently at 80 Hz than at 8 kHz.
At higher frequencies, reflections often create audible changes in clarity, stereo imaging, brightness, and reverberation.
At low frequencies, the entire room begins to behave more like a resonant pressure system. Reflections from large boundaries combine with the direct sound and create strong peaks and dips.
The sound reaching the listener is therefore not simply the signal emitted by the loudspeaker.
It is closer to:
Basic relationship
Heard Sound = Direct Sound + Reflections + Room Resonances
The direct sound arrives first. Reflections arrive later after travelling additional distances. Each reflected path introduces its own delay and phase relationship.
At some frequencies, reflected energy reinforces the direct signal.
At others, it partially cancels it.
This is why the same speaker can sound balanced in one room and boomy or weak in another.
The room becomes part of the playback system.
Practical example
Imagine a speaker reproducing a steady 80 Hz tone.
The direct wave reaches your listening position first. Another portion travels toward the rear wall, reflects, and then reaches you slightly later.
If the reflected wave arrives in phase with the direct wave, the 80 Hz tone becomes stronger.
If it arrives closer to opposite phase, the tone becomes weaker.
Move your chair forward by less than a metre and the relationship may change again.
Take away
 A room changes sound through reflection, absorption, transmission, and scattering.
 Different frequencies interact with surfaces differently.
 Bass is especially influenced by large room boundaries.
 The sound you hear is a combination of direct and reflected energy.

lessons.title: Standing Waves and Room Modes
lessons.body:
In an enclosed room, low-frequency sound repeatedly reflects between boundaries.
When the dimensions of the room are related to particular wavelengths, reflected waves can repeatedly reinforce themselves. This creates a resonant pattern called a room mode.
Instead of energy spreading evenly, the room develops areas of high and low acoustic pressure.
These patterns are often described as standing waves.
A standing wave does not appear to travel through the room in the same way as a free-moving wave. Instead, the pressure pattern remains relatively fixed in space.
Some locations become pressure maxima.
Others become pressure minima.
This explains a common listening experience: one bass note may sound extremely strong near a wall but almost disappear at another position.
The simplest room modes occur between two parallel boundaries.
For example, consider a room that is 4 metres long.
The fundamental axial mode along this dimension can be estimated using:
Formula
f = c / 2L
Where:
f = modal frequency
c = speed of sound
L = room dimension
For a 4 m room:
f = 343 / (2 × 4)
f ≈ 42.9 Hz
That means the room may strongly support a resonance around 43 Hz along that dimension.
Higher-order modes occur at integer multiples:
2 × 42.9 ≈ 85.8 Hz
3 × 42.9 ≈ 128.7 Hz
A real room has three major dimensions:
 length
 width
 height
Each creates its own family of modes.
These modal families overlap, creating a complex low-frequency response.
Room modes are usually divided into three main categories.
Axial modes
These involve reflections between two opposite surfaces.
Examples:
 front wall ↔ rear wall
 left wall ↔ right wall
 floor ↔ ceiling
They are usually the strongest individual modes.
Tangential modes
These involve four surfaces.
They generally contain less energy than axial modes.
Oblique modes
These involve all six major room surfaces and are usually weaker individually, though many can exist.
The lower the frequency, the more separated individual room modes tend to be.
At higher frequencies, modal density increases and the resonances overlap so heavily that the room behaves more statistically.
Practical example
A room measures:
5 m × 4 m × 2.5 m
Approximate fundamental axial modes are:
Length:
343 / (2 × 5) ≈ 34.3 Hz
Width:
343 / (2 × 4) ≈ 42.9 Hz
Height:
343 / (2 × 2.5) ≈ 68.6 Hz
These frequencies may become particularly important when placing subwoofers and choosing a listening position.
Take away
 Room modes are resonances created by room dimensions.
 Standing waves create fixed regions of high and low pressure.
 Axial modes usually have the strongest individual effect.
 Every room dimension produces its own modal frequencies.
 Low-frequency response can vary greatly with position.

lessons.title: Peaks, Nulls and Why Bass Disappears
lessons.body:
One of the most confusing things about bass is that increasing the volume does not always fix a weak frequency.
Sometimes the problem is not insufficient output.
It is cancellation.
When direct and reflected sound arrive with opposing phase relationships, they can reduce each other. The result is a null — a location where a frequency becomes much quieter than expected.
The opposite can also happen.
When several arrivals reinforce each other, they create a peak.
A peak may make one note sound disproportionately loud or boomy.
A null may make another note feel almost absent.
This creates a frequency response that is uneven across the room.
Suppose your system produces 60 Hz correctly, but at your listening position a strong cancellation occurs.
Turning the subwoofer up by 6 dB increases both the direct and reflected sound.
The cancellation relationship remains.
You may increase the overall bass level while the missing 60 Hz frequency remains unusually weak.
This is why equalization alone cannot reliably fix a deep acoustic null.
The more effective solution may involve:
 moving the listener
 moving the subwoofer
 using multiple subwoofers
 changing delay or phase
 changing room treatment
A peak is usually easier to reduce electronically because excess energy can be attenuated.
A deep null is different because the energy is cancelling acoustically.
Simplified example
Imagine two equal 70 Hz signals arriving at the same point.
Signal A:
+1
Signal B:
−1
Combined:
+1 + (−1) = 0
This is an idealized example of complete cancellation.
In a real room, cancellation is rarely perfect, but reductions of 10, 20, or even more decibels can occur at certain positions and frequencies.
Why small movements matter
At high frequencies, moving your head a few centimetres can change the phase relationship significantly because wavelengths are short.
At bass frequencies, larger movements are usually required, but even a movement of 30–50 cm can noticeably change some frequencies.
A seat located directly inside a modal null may therefore be much worse than another seat nearby.
Practical example
You play a bass sweep from 30 Hz to 120 Hz.
At 45 Hz, the room feels powerful.
At 70 Hz, the bass nearly disappears.
At 95 Hz, it becomes strong again.
The loudspeaker is not necessarily faulty. The room and listening position are creating a frequency-dependent combination of peaks and nulls.
Take away
 Peaks are caused by constructive interference.
 Nulls are caused by destructive interference.
 Deep nulls cannot always be solved by simply increasing volume.
 Position changes can be more effective than EQ.
 Bass response should be measured or evaluated across multiple frequencies.

lessons.title: Boundary Gain and Speaker Placement
lessons.body:
The position of a loudspeaker relative to walls changes how much low-frequency energy reaches the listener.
A loudspeaker in open space radiates sound in many directions.
When it is placed close to a large boundary, some of the energy that would have travelled behind the speaker is reflected back into the room.
At low frequencies, where the wavelength is large, the direct and reflected energy can combine strongly.
This effect is commonly called boundary gain or boundary reinforcement.
Moving a bass source closer to a wall can increase low-frequency output.
Moving it into a corner can increase reinforcement further because multiple boundaries are involved.
This is one reason subwoofers are often placed near walls or corners when additional output is needed.
However, increased output is not automatically better.
The same position that provides more level may also excite certain room modes more strongly.
A corner may produce powerful bass but also exaggerate specific frequencies.
A more central position may sound smoother but provide less efficiency.
Placement is therefore a balance between:
 output
 modal excitation
 frequency smoothness
 seat-to-seat consistency
Speaker-boundary interference
Another placement effect occurs when reflected sound from a nearby wall combines with the direct sound.
This is often called speaker-boundary interference response, or SBIR.
The reflected path is longer than the direct path.
At frequencies where that path difference corresponds to approximately half a wavelength, the reflected sound may arrive out of phase and create a cancellation.
A simplified relationship is:
Formula
f ≈ c / 2Δd
Where:
Δd = difference between the direct and reflected path lengths
The exact geometry can be more complicated, but the principle remains the same.
Changing the distance between the speaker and the wall moves the cancellation frequency.
This is why moving a speaker only 20 or 30 centimetres can sometimes produce a surprisingly large change in low-mid or bass response.
Practical example
A subwoofer is placed close to the front wall and produces strong output, but one frequency around 70 Hz is excessive.
Moving the subwoofer farther along the wall may excite the room differently.
Alternatively, placing a second subwoofer at another position may help distribute energy more evenly.
Take away
 Nearby walls can reinforce low-frequency output.
 Corners can provide even stronger boundary reinforcement.
 More bass level does not always mean smoother bass.
 Speaker-to-wall distance can create cancellation effects.
 Placement should be optimized for response, not only maximum output.
 Multiple positions should be tested before relying on EQ.

lessons.title: Finding a Better Listening Position
lessons.body:
The listening position is just as important as the speaker position.
A perfectly capable system can sound poor if the listener is sitting inside a strong room-mode null or peak.
This is especially important below roughly 100–150 Hz, where room behavior is strongly dominated by resonances and boundary interactions.
A common mistake is to place the listening position exactly against a wall.
Near many boundaries, low-frequency pressure can increase substantially. This may create exaggerated bass and make it difficult to judge the system accurately.
Another problematic location can be the exact geometric centre of the room.
Depending on room dimensions, the centre may coincide with nulls of several axial modes.
This does not mean that every room behaves identically, but it is a useful reason to test multiple positions instead of choosing one based only on furniture symmetry.
A practical approach is to move the listening position gradually while playing low-frequency sweeps or familiar bass-heavy material.
Listen for:
 notes that suddenly become louder
 notes that disappear
 changes in bass tightness
 differences between left and right
 whether bass feels concentrated in one frequency range
For more accurate work, a measurement microphone can be used to compare frequency-response curves at different positions.
The objective is not necessarily to find a location with perfectly flat response.
Real rooms rarely provide that naturally.
The goal is to find a position with fewer extreme peaks and deep nulls, making later correction easier.
The subwoofer crawl concept
A commonly used practical technique is called the subwoofer crawl.
The basic idea is to temporarily place the subwoofer near the normal listening position and then move around the room while bass material plays.
Locations where the bass sounds relatively even may be good candidates for subwoofer placement.
The method is not mathematically perfect, but it can be a useful starting point in rooms where measurement equipment is unavailable.
Measurement strategy
A more systematic method is:
 Choose several possible listening positions.
 Measure the response at each position.
 Compare major peaks and nulls.
 Avoid positions with very deep cancellations.
 Move the subwoofer and repeat.
 Apply EQ only after placement is reasonably optimized.
This order matters.
Physical placement should usually be addressed before aggressive electronic correction.
Practical example
At Position A, the response shows:
45 Hz: +8 dB
70 Hz: −18 dB
95 Hz: +5 dB
At Position B:
45 Hz: +4 dB
70 Hz: −6 dB
95 Hz: +3 dB
Position B may be the better starting point even if it does not look perfectly flat, because the deep 70 Hz null is much smaller and easier to manage.
Take away
 Listener position strongly affects bass response.
 Avoid choosing a seat based only on room symmetry.
 Deep nulls are usually harder to correct than moderate peaks.
 Test several positions before applying EQ.
 Measurement can reveal problems that are difficult to identify by ear.

title: Frequency, Harmonics & Timbre
description: This module explains why two sounds with the same fundamental frequency can sound completely different, how harmonics shape tone, what overtones and partials are, how filters change frequency content, and why the spectral structure of a sound matters as much as its pitch.

lessons.title: Fundamental Frequency and Harmonics
lessons.body:
A musical or tonal sound is rarely made from only one frequency.
When a string, vocal cord, loudspeaker, or other vibrating system produces a stable tone, one frequency usually dominates our perception of pitch. This frequency is called the fundamental frequency.
If a tone has a fundamental frequency of:
100 Hz
we usually perceive its pitch as being based around 100 Hz.
But the sound may also contain energy at:
200 Hz
300 Hz
400 Hz
500 Hz
and many higher frequencies.
These additional frequency components are called harmonics when they occur at integer multiples of the fundamental.
Harmonic relationship
If the fundamental frequency is:
f₀
then the harmonic frequencies are:
2f₀, 3f₀, 4f₀, 5f₀...
For a 100 Hz fundamental:
1st harmonic = 100 Hz
2nd harmonic = 200 Hz
3rd harmonic = 300 Hz
4th harmonic = 400 Hz
5th harmonic = 500 Hz
The first harmonic is usually the fundamental itself.
The relative strength of these harmonics determines much of the character of the sound.
A nearly pure sine wave contains mostly one frequency.
A richer sound may contain many harmonics at different amplitudes.
This is one of the main reasons a bass guitar, synthesizer, piano, and human voice can all produce approximately the same musical note while sounding completely different.
The pitch may be similar, but the harmonic structure is not.
Harmonic amplitude matters
It is not enough to know which harmonics exist.
Their amplitudes also matter.
Imagine two sounds with the same 100 Hz fundamental.
Sound A:
100 Hz = strong
200 Hz = weak
300 Hz = very weak
Sound B:
100 Hz = strong
200 Hz = strong
300 Hz = moderate
400 Hz = moderate
500 Hz = weak
Both may be perceived as having the same basic pitch, but Sound B will usually feel brighter, richer, or more complex.
Why harmonics matter in bass
Harmonics are particularly important for low-frequency sounds.
A bass note may have a fundamental frequency so low that small speakers reproduce it poorly. However, the higher harmonics can still help the brain recognize the note.
This is one reason bass can sometimes remain perceptually identifiable even when the deepest fundamental is weak.
Practical example
Consider an 80 Hz bass note.
Its first few harmonics are:
80 Hz
160 Hz
240 Hz
320 Hz
400 Hz
If the 80 Hz component is strong but the upper harmonics are weak, the tone may sound smooth and deep.
If 160 Hz, 240 Hz, and 320 Hz are stronger, the bass may sound more defined or aggressive.
Take away
 The fundamental frequency strongly influences perceived pitch.
 Harmonics occur at integer multiples of the fundamental.
 Harmonic balance changes the character of a sound.
 Bass definition often depends on frequencies above the fundamental.

lessons.title: Timbre: Why Equal Notes Sound Different
lessons.body:
Timbre is the quality that allows us to distinguish different sound sources even when they play the same pitch at a similar loudness.
If a piano and a guitar both play the same note, we can usually identify which instrument is which almost immediately.
The difference is not mainly the fundamental frequency.
It is the combination of:
 harmonic content
 amplitude envelope
 transient behavior
 noise components
 resonance
 modulation
 phase relationships
 spectral evolution over time
Together, these characteristics create timbre.
Timbre is sometimes described as the “color” of sound, but physically it is better understood as the combination of spectral and time-domain characteristics that make a sound recognizable.
Static spectrum is not enough
Imagine two sounds that contain the same frequencies.
If one sound begins instantly and the other fades in slowly, they may still sound very different.
This is because our perception is sensitive not only to which frequencies are present, but also to how they change over time.
A drum hit may contain a very short, bright transient followed by a fast decay.
A bowed string may build more gradually and sustain for much longer.
A synthesizer pad may have a slow attack and long release.
The frequency spectrum of all three may overlap significantly, yet their perceived character is very different.
Envelope
A common model for describing the shape of a sound over time is:
ADSR
This stands for:
Attack
Decay
Sustain
Release
Attack describes how quickly the sound rises from silence.
Decay describes how it moves from the initial peak toward the sustained level.
Sustain describes the level maintained while the sound continues.
Release describes how the sound fades after the source stops.
Example
A plucked bass note may have:
 fast attack
 short decay
 moderate sustain
 medium release
A soft synth pad may have:
 slow attack
 long decay
 high sustain
 long release
Even if both contain similar low-frequency fundamentals, their temporal shapes make them feel entirely different.
Practical example
Take a 100 Hz sine wave.
First, play it with an immediate attack and immediate stop.
Then play the same 100 Hz tone with a 500 ms fade-in and a 1 second fade-out.
The frequency is unchanged, but the subjective character becomes much softer and less percussive.
Take away
 Timbre is more than pitch.
 Harmonic balance helps define sound identity.
 The amplitude envelope changes how a sound is perceived.
 Transients are especially important for recognizing many instruments.
 Two sounds can share a pitch but have very different timbres.

lessons.title: Overtones, Partials and Inharmonic Content
lessons.body:
The words harmonic, overtone, and partial are often used interchangeably, but they do not mean exactly the same thing.
A partial is any individual sinusoidal component within a complex sound.
A harmonic is a partial whose frequency is an integer multiple of the fundamental.
An overtone is any frequency component above the fundamental.
This creates an important numbering difference.
If the fundamental is 100 Hz:
Fundamental / 1st harmonic = 100 Hz
1st overtone / 2nd harmonic = 200 Hz
2nd overtone / 3rd harmonic = 300 Hz
So the overtone number is usually one lower than the harmonic number.
Not every sound is perfectly harmonic
Many musical sounds contain mostly harmonic frequency relationships.
However, some instruments and physical objects create strong inharmonic partials.
These are frequency components that are not exact integer multiples of the fundamental.
Bells are a classic example.
Their vibration patterns can produce partials with more complicated frequency relationships.
Percussion instruments can also contain significant inharmonic content.
This often gives them a metallic, noisy, or complex character.
Harmonic series
A perfectly harmonic series follows:
fₙ = n × f₀
Where:
fₙ = frequency of harmonic n
n = harmonic number
f₀ = fundamental frequency
For a 70 Hz bass tone:
1 × 70 = 70 Hz
2 × 70 = 140 Hz
3 × 70 = 210 Hz
4 × 70 = 280 Hz
5 × 70 = 350 Hz
These relationships are mathematically simple, but the amplitude of each component can vary greatly.
Missing fundamental effect
Human hearing can sometimes perceive a pitch even when the physical fundamental frequency is absent.
Suppose a sound contains:
200 Hz
300 Hz
400 Hz
500 Hz
These frequencies correspond to harmonics of a hypothetical 100 Hz fundamental.
Even if 100 Hz itself is missing, the auditory system may still interpret the sound as having a pitch related to 100 Hz.
This phenomenon is often called the missing fundamental.
It is important in telecommunication, speaker design, psychoacoustics, and bass reproduction.
Small speakers may not reproduce a very low fundamental efficiently, but carefully preserved harmonics can still help listeners infer the intended pitch.
Practical example
Imagine a bass note with a fundamental at 50 Hz.
Its harmonics include:
100 Hz
150 Hz
200 Hz
250 Hz
If a small speaker cannot reproduce 50 Hz effectively but can reproduce the higher harmonics, the note may still be recognizable as a low bass note.
The physical 50 Hz energy is weaker, but the harmonic pattern provides enough information for the brain to infer the pitch.
Take away
 A partial is any individual spectral component.
 Harmonics follow integer multiples of the fundamental.
 Overtones are components above the fundamental.
 Some sounds contain important inharmonic partials.
 The brain can sometimes infer a missing fundamental from higher harmonics.
 Harmonic structure can preserve pitch information even when deep bass is weak.

lessons.title: Sine, Square, Triangle and Sawtooth Waves
lessons.body:
Basic waveform shapes are useful because they demonstrate how harmonic content changes the character of a sound.
Four commonly discussed waveforms are:
 sine
 square
 triangle
 sawtooth
Each can repeat at the same fundamental frequency while producing a very different timbre.
Sine wave
A sine wave is the simplest periodic waveform.
Ideally, it contains only one frequency.
A 100 Hz sine wave contains:
100 Hz
with no harmonic series in the ideal mathematical case.
Because of this, sine waves sound smooth, pure, and relatively simple.
They are commonly used for:
 testing speakers
 measuring frequency response
 checking resonances
 studying phase
 generating reference tones
Square wave
A square wave contains the fundamental plus odd harmonics.
Its harmonic series includes approximately:
f₀
3f₀
5f₀
7f₀
For a 100 Hz square wave:
100 Hz
300 Hz
500 Hz
700 Hz
The amplitude of higher harmonics decreases as harmonic number increases.
This rich high-frequency content gives the square wave a bright and buzzy character.
Triangle wave
A triangle wave also contains primarily odd harmonics:
f₀, 3f₀, 5f₀, 7f₀...
but the harmonic amplitudes decrease much faster than in a square wave.
As a result, a triangle wave sounds softer and less bright.
It still has more harmonic complexity than a sine wave, but significantly less than a square wave.
Sawtooth wave
A sawtooth wave contains both odd and even harmonics.
Its harmonic sequence includes:
f₀
2f₀
3f₀
4f₀
5f₀
This dense harmonic content makes sawtooth waves sound bright, rich, and aggressive.
They are extremely common in synthesis because filtering a harmonically rich waveform provides many possibilities for shaping tone.
Same pitch, different spectrum
Suppose all four waveforms use a fundamental frequency of 100 Hz.
They all repeat 100 times per second.
Yet their spectra are different.
That means their pitch can be perceived as similar while their timbre changes dramatically.
This demonstrates an important principle:
Waveform shape and frequency spectrum are two views of the same signal.
A more complex waveform in the time domain generally corresponds to a richer set of frequency components in the frequency domain.
Practical example
Play four tones at 100 Hz:
 sine
 triangle
 square
 sawtooth
Keep their perceived loudness as similar as possible.
The sine sounds smooth.
The triangle sounds slightly richer.
The square sounds hollow and bright.
The sawtooth sounds dense and aggressive.
Their fundamental frequency is identical. Their harmonic content creates the difference.
Take away
 A sine wave contains one ideal frequency.
 Square waves contain strong odd harmonics.
 Triangle waves contain weaker odd harmonics.
 Sawtooth waves contain both odd and even harmonics.
 Waveform shape strongly affects timbre.
 Signals with the same fundamental can sound dramatically different.
 Rich waveforms are useful starting points for synthesis.

lessons.title: Frequency Spectrum and Spectrum Analysis
lessons.body:
A waveform shows how a signal changes over time.
A spectrum shows how the signal's energy is distributed across frequency.
Both views describe the same signal, but they answer different questions.
A waveform can show:
 timing
 transients
 amplitude changes
 clipping
 pauses
 periodicity
A spectrum can show:
 fundamental frequency
 harmonics
 noise
 resonances
 frequency balance
 tonal peaks
For sound analysis, it is often useful to switch between both views.
Frequency-domain representation
Imagine a recorded bass note.
The waveform may look complicated.
In the frequency spectrum, you might see clear peaks at:
60 Hz
120 Hz
180 Hz
240 Hz
This immediately reveals a fundamental around 60 Hz with several harmonics.
Another recording might show a broad, continuous spread of energy instead of narrow peaks.
This may indicate noise or a complex transient signal.
FFT
Many digital spectrum analyzers use the Fast Fourier Transform, or FFT.
The FFT is an efficient algorithm for converting a block of time-domain samples into a frequency-domain representation.
Conceptually, it answers the question:
Which sinusoidal frequencies are present in this signal, and how strong are they?
The analyzer divides the spectrum into frequency bins.
The number and spacing of these bins depend on:
 sample rate
 FFT size
 analysis window
 time duration
Frequency resolution
A simplified relationship is:
Δf = Fs / N
Where:
Δf = spacing between frequency bins
Fs = sample rate
N = FFT size
For:
Fs = 48,000 Hz
N = 4096
we get:
Δf = 48,000 / 4096 ≈ 11.72 Hz
A larger FFT size provides finer frequency resolution.
However, there is a trade-off.
To analyze more samples, the system needs a longer time window.
This can reduce how quickly the spectrum responds to fast changes.
Time versus frequency resolution
Short analysis windows provide better timing information but poorer frequency precision.
Long windows provide better frequency precision but average the signal across more time.
This trade-off is fundamental to audio analysis.
There is no single perfect FFT setting for every task.
Analyzing a slowly changing bass tone may benefit from a longer window.
Analyzing a short drum transient may require better time resolution.
Practical example
You record a note that appears to be around 50 Hz.
A spectrum analyzer shows strong peaks at:
49 Hz
98 Hz
147 Hz
196 Hz
The pattern strongly suggests a fundamental near 49 Hz with harmonic multiples above it.
This is far easier to identify in a spectrum than from the raw waveform alone.
Take away
 A waveform shows signal behavior over time.
 A spectrum shows energy across frequencies.
 FFT analysis separates complex signals into frequency components.
 Larger FFT sizes improve frequency resolution.
 Analysis settings involve a trade-off between time and frequency detail.

lessons.title: Filters and Frequency Shaping
lessons.body:
A filter changes a signal by reducing or emphasizing selected frequency regions.
Filters are used almost everywhere in audio:
 equalizers
 crossovers
 synthesizers
 loudspeakers
 microphones
 effects
 room correction
 mastering
 measurement systems
The most basic filter categories are:
 low-pass
 high-pass
 band-pass
 band-stop
Low-pass filter
A low-pass filter allows frequencies below a selected region to pass more easily while attenuating higher frequencies.
For example, a low-pass filter set near 100 Hz may allow bass frequencies through while reducing midrange and treble.
This is commonly used in subwoofer systems.
High-pass filter
A high-pass filter does the opposite.
It allows higher frequencies through while attenuating frequencies below the cutoff region.
A high-pass filter may be used to remove:
 subsonic rumble
 handling noise
 unnecessary deep bass
 low-frequency energy from small speakers
Band-pass filter
A band-pass filter allows a selected range of frequencies while attenuating frequencies below and above that range.
It can isolate a particular part of a spectrum.
Band-stop filter
A band-stop filter attenuates a selected frequency range while leaving frequencies on either side less affected.
A very narrow band-stop filter is often called a notch filter.
Notch filters can be useful for reducing narrow resonances or unwanted tones.
Cutoff frequency
The cutoff frequency is usually associated with the transition region between the pass band and the attenuated region.
A filter does not normally remove everything immediately at one exact frequency.
Instead, attenuation increases gradually.
The rate at which this happens is called the slope.
Common slopes include:
6 dB/octave
12 dB/octave
18 dB/octave
24 dB/octave
A steeper slope attenuates frequencies more rapidly beyond the cutoff region.
Example
Imagine a low-pass filter at 100 Hz with a slope of 12 dB/octave.
If the response is approximately at its reference level around 100 Hz, then one octave above:
200 Hz
the signal may be about 12 dB lower.
Another octave above:
400 Hz
it may be approximately another 12 dB lower.
Real filter behavior depends on the exact design, but this illustrates the concept.
Filters and phase
Filters do more than change amplitude.
Many filter designs also change phase near the cutoff region.
This becomes important when combining multiple speakers or signal paths.
For example, a subwoofer low-pass filter and a main-speaker high-pass filter must work together around the crossover frequency.
If their amplitude and phase relationships are poorly aligned, the combined response may contain a peak or cancellation.
Practical example
A subwoofer produces useful output up to 150 Hz, but the main speakers already reproduce that range strongly.
A low-pass filter is applied to the subwoofer around 80 Hz.
The goal is to let the subwoofer focus on deep bass while the main speakers handle the upper bass and midrange.
The exact crossover point and slope should be chosen according to the system, not from a universal number.
Take away
 Filters reshape the frequency content of a signal.
 Low-pass filters reduce higher frequencies.
 High-pass filters reduce lower frequencies.
 Band-pass filters isolate a frequency region.
 Filter slope controls how quickly attenuation increases.
 Filters can also change phase near the crossover region.

lessons.title: Equalization and Spectral Balance
lessons.body:
Equalization, usually shortened to EQ, is the process of changing the level of selected frequency regions.
EQ can be used for many purposes:
 correcting tonal imbalance
 reducing resonances
 making speech clearer
 shaping an instrument
 compensating for a loudspeaker response
 adjusting a system to a room
 creating deliberate tonal effects
An equalizer does not simply make sound “better.”
It changes the spectrum.
Whether that change is useful depends on the problem being solved.
Common EQ parameters
A parametric EQ usually provides three key controls:
Frequency
Gain
Q
Frequency selects the center of the adjustment.
Gain determines how much the selected region is boosted or reduced.
Q controls the width of the affected region.
A high Q value creates a narrower adjustment.
A low Q value affects a broader frequency region.
Narrow versus broad EQ
Suppose a measurement reveals a narrow resonance at:
72 Hz
A relatively narrow EQ cut may reduce that resonance without strongly affecting neighboring frequencies.
If the entire low-mid region from approximately 150 Hz to 400 Hz sounds too heavy, a broader EQ adjustment may be more appropriate.
The shape of the problem should guide the shape of the correction.
Boost versus cut
Cuts are often easier to use safely than large boosts.
If a room creates a strong 50 Hz peak, reducing that frequency with EQ can lower excess energy.
If the room creates a deep 70 Hz null through cancellation, applying a large boost may accomplish very little.
For example:
The room creates a:
−18 dB null at 70 Hz
Adding:
+12 dB EQ
does not necessarily produce a clean 12 dB improvement.
The direct and reflected energy may still cancel at that position.
Meanwhile, the amplifier and loudspeaker are being asked to produce much more energy.
This wastes headroom and can increase distortion.
EQ cannot replace placement
Electronic correction is most effective after major physical problems have been addressed.
A practical sequence is:
 choose speaker positions
 choose listening positions
 adjust subwoofer placement
 align multiple sources
 measure the response
 identify correctable peaks
 apply moderate EQ
 re-measure
This avoids using EQ to fight problems that are fundamentally spatial.
Spectral balance
A technically flat response is not always the same as a subjectively ideal response.
Perception depends on:
 listening level
 room acoustics
 speaker directivity
 source material
 individual hearing
 playback purpose
For example, a system designed for casual listening may use a different target balance than a studio monitoring system.
The important concept is that EQ should have a defined purpose.
A correction should answer a question such as:
What measurable or audible problem am I trying to change?
Without that question, random boosts and cuts can make the system less predictable rather than better.
Practical example
A measurement shows:
45 Hz: +7 dB
70 Hz: −14 dB
95 Hz: +5 dB
A reasonable approach may be:
 reduce the 45 Hz peak
 avoid aggressively boosting the 70 Hz null
 investigate placement for the 70 Hz issue
 reduce the 95 Hz peak if it is consistently audible
 re-measure after each important change
The goal is not to force every point on the graph into a perfectly straight line.
The goal is to create a smoother, more useful acoustic result without wasting system headroom.
Take away
 EQ changes the level of selected frequency regions.
 Parametric EQ commonly uses frequency, gain, and Q.
 Narrow problems usually require narrow corrections.
 Deep acoustic nulls are poor candidates for large boosts.
 Placement and alignment should usually come before heavy EQ.
 Measure before and after making important corrections.
 A useful EQ change should solve a defined problem.
 Perfect graphical flatness is not always the only meaningful target.

title: Digital Audio, Recording & Signal Flow
description: This module explains how physical sound becomes digital audio, how microphones capture pressure changes, what sample rate and bit depth mean, why clipping occurs, how recording level affects quality, and what happens when audio is reversed or processed inside an application.

lessons.title: From Air Pressure to Digital Audio
lessons.body:
A sound begins as a physical event.
A voice, loudspeaker, instrument, or moving object creates variations in air pressure. Before a phone or computer can store that sound, those pressure variations must be converted into an electrical and then a digital representation.
A microphone performs the first important conversion.
Its diaphragm moves in response to changes in acoustic pressure. The microphone converts this mechanical movement into an electrical signal whose voltage changes over time.
The electrical signal is still continuous.
A digital device cannot store an infinitely detailed continuous waveform directly. Instead, it measures the signal repeatedly at extremely short time intervals.
This process is called sampling.
Each measurement records the amplitude of the signal at one moment.
The sequence of these measurements forms a digital representation of the original waveform.
The conversion process can be summarized as:
Acoustic Pressure → Microphone → Electrical Signal → ADC → Digital Samples
ADC means Analog-to-Digital Converter.
The reverse process happens during playback.
Stored digital samples are sent through a Digital-to-Analog Converter, or DAC.
The DAC reconstructs an analog electrical signal, an amplifier provides the required power, and a loudspeaker converts that electrical signal back into mechanical movement and acoustic pressure.
Recording chain
A simplified recording chain is:
Sound Source → Air → Microphone → Preamplifier → ADC → Digital Audio
A playback chain might be:
Digital Audio → DAC → Amplifier → Speaker → Air → Listener
Every stage can affect the resulting sound.
The microphone has its own frequency response and directional characteristics.
The preamplifier adds gain.
The converter has technical limitations.
The room introduces reflections.
The listener's position changes the acoustic result.
This means a recording is never simply a perfect copy of the original event. It is a representation produced by an entire signal chain.
Waveform representation
Once audio is digital, it can be displayed as a waveform.
The horizontal axis usually represents:
Time
The vertical axis usually represents:
Amplitude
Large vertical movement indicates larger signal amplitude.
Small movement indicates lower amplitude.
A waveform can help you identify:
 silence
 loud sections
 transients
 clipping
 timing
 repeated patterns
However, a waveform does not directly show which frequencies are present.
For that, a spectrum or spectrogram is usually more useful.
Practical example
Record yourself saying one short word.
The microphone diaphragm moves with the changing pressure from your voice.
The phone samples the electrical representation thousands of times per second.
When you look at the recorded waveform, the louder vowel portions usually appear larger than quiet pauses or soft consonants.
The waveform is not a picture of your voice itself. It is a time-based representation of the recorded signal amplitude.
Take away
 Microphones convert acoustic pressure into electrical signals.
 An ADC converts analog signals into digital samples.
 Digital audio is a sequence of amplitude measurements over time.
 A waveform shows how amplitude changes through time.
 Playback reverses the conversion process and returns the signal to physical sound.

lessons.title: Sample Rate and the Nyquist Limit
lessons.body:
Sample rate describes how many measurements of an analog audio signal are taken every second during digital conversion.
It is measured in samples per second, usually written in hertz or kilohertz.
Common sample rates include:
44.1 kHz
48 kHz
88.2 kHz
96 kHz
A sample rate of:
48 kHz
means that the system records:
48,000 samples every second
Each sample stores the signal's amplitude at a particular moment.
A higher sample rate means the waveform is measured more frequently.
However, sample rate should not be understood simply as “more samples always means more audible quality.”
There is an important mathematical limit.
Nyquist frequency
According to the sampling theorem, a sampled system must use a sample rate greater than twice the highest frequency that needs to be represented.
A simplified relationship is:
fmax < Fs / 2
Where:
fmax = highest reproducible frequency
Fs = sample rate
The quantity:
Fs / 2
is called the Nyquist frequency.
For a 48 kHz sample rate:
48,000 / 2 = 24,000 Hz
So the theoretical Nyquist frequency is:
24 kHz
For 44.1 kHz:
44,100 / 2 = 22,050 Hz
This is one reason common audio sample rates are slightly above twice the upper range typically associated with human hearing.
Why frequencies above Nyquist are a problem
If a frequency above the Nyquist limit enters the sampling process without proper filtering, it can be represented incorrectly as a lower frequency.
This phenomenon is called aliasing.
Aliasing creates frequency components that were not part of the intended signal.
For this reason, real digital recording systems use anti-aliasing filters before or as part of conversion.
These filters reduce frequencies that cannot be represented correctly at the chosen sample rate.
Simple aliasing concept
Suppose a system uses an extremely low sample rate.
The waveform may be measured too slowly to determine its true frequency.
A rapidly oscillating signal can then appear to be a completely different, slower oscillation.
This is similar to how a rotating wheel in video can sometimes appear to rotate backward because the camera captures frames at particular intervals.
Digital audio aliasing follows a related sampling principle.
Does higher sample rate change pitch?
No.
Recording a 440 Hz tone at 48 kHz does not make it a different pitch from recording the same correctly sampled tone at 96 kHz.
The fundamental frequency is still 440 Hz.
The sample rate determines how the continuous signal is represented digitally, not the musical pitch of a properly recorded source.
Sample rate and file size
Higher sample rates also produce more data.
If all other factors remain equal:
96 kHz
requires twice as many samples per second as:
48 kHz
This increases:
 storage requirements
 processing load
 memory bandwidth
 data transfer
Therefore, sample-rate selection is a technical trade-off rather than a simple quality slider.
Practical example
A recording uses:
48,000 samples per second
Its theoretical Nyquist frequency is:
24,000 Hz
A 10 kHz component can be represented because it is below the limit.
A 30 kHz component is above the Nyquist frequency and must be filtered before sampling to prevent aliasing into the audible spectrum.
Take away
 Sample rate is the number of digital samples captured per second.
 48 kHz means 48,000 samples every second.
 The Nyquist frequency is half the sample rate.
 Frequencies above Nyquist can create aliasing.
 Anti-aliasing filters protect the digital recording process.
 Higher sample rates increase data and processing requirements.

lessons.title: Bit Depth, Dynamic Range and Quantization
lessons.body:
Sample rate determines how often the signal is measured.
Bit depth determines how many possible amplitude values can be assigned to each sample.
These are separate concepts.
Sample rate concerns the horizontal, time-related resolution of a digital signal.
Bit depth concerns the available amplitude levels.
Common PCM audio bit depths include:
16-bit
24-bit
An ideal N-bit system has approximately:
2ᴺ
possible digital values.
For 16-bit audio:
2¹⁶ = 65,536 levels
For 24-bit audio:
2²⁴ = 16,777,216 levels
The system maps the analog signal to the nearest available digital value.
This process is called quantization.
Quantization error
Because digital amplitude values are discrete, the measured signal cannot always match the exact analog amplitude.
The difference between the actual continuous value and the stored digital value is called quantization error.
In a well-designed audio system, this behaves as a very low-level noise-like component rather than simply destroying the waveform.
Greater bit depth provides more available amplitude levels and a lower theoretical quantization noise floor.
Approximate dynamic range
A commonly used approximation for ideal PCM dynamic range is:
Dynamic Range ≈ 6.02N + 1.76 dB
Where:
N = number of bits
For 16-bit audio:
6.02 × 16 + 1.76 ≈ 98 dB
For 24-bit audio:
6.02 × 24 + 1.76 ≈ 146 dB
These are theoretical values for ideal quantization.
Real recording systems also contain:
 microphone self-noise
 preamplifier noise
 converter noise
 environmental noise
 electronic limitations
So the usable real-world dynamic range is usually lower than the ideal mathematical number.
Why 24-bit is useful during recording
A major advantage of 24-bit recording is not that every recording suddenly sounds dramatically different.
It gives engineers more practical headroom between normal recording levels and the digital noise floor.
This means you can record at safer levels without needing to push the signal extremely close to digital maximum.
That makes gain staging easier and reduces the temptation to record too hot.
Bit depth and loudness
Bit depth does not directly determine how loud a sound plays.
Playback loudness depends on the signal level and playback system.
A 16-bit and 24-bit recording can reproduce the same nominal audio level.
The major difference is the precision and available dynamic range of the digital representation.
Practical example
Imagine recording speech.
If you aim for sensible peaks well below digital clipping while using a 24-bit recording path, you retain plenty of digital resolution.
There is usually no need to push every peak close to 0 dBFS merely to “use all the bits.”
Modern digital recording benefits from leaving headroom.
Take away
 Bit depth determines the available digital amplitude values.
 Higher bit depth provides greater theoretical dynamic range.
 Quantization maps continuous amplitudes to discrete values.
 24-bit recording gives useful headroom for practical recording.
 Bit depth does not directly determine playback loudness.

lessons.title: Recording Levels, Headroom and Clipping
lessons.body:
Every digital recording system has a maximum representable signal level.
In digital audio, this maximum is commonly referenced as:
0 dBFS
The letters FS mean Full Scale.
A digital signal cannot normally exceed 0 dBFS within a conventional fixed digital representation.
If the incoming analog signal is amplified too strongly before conversion, the required digital value exceeds the available maximum.
The peaks are then clipped.
What clipping does
Imagine a sine wave that should rise smoothly toward its positive peak.
If the recording system reaches its maximum value before the waveform reaches its natural peak, the top of the waveform is cut off.
The same happens at negative peaks.
Instead of a smooth shape, the waveform develops flattened sections.
This introduces additional harmonic content and distortion.
The more severe the clipping, the more obvious the audible change can become.
Headroom
Headroom is the safety margin between normal signal peaks and the maximum available level.
For example, if a recording reaches peaks around:
−12 dBFS
there is approximately 12 dB of digital peak headroom before reaching 0 dBFS.
Leaving headroom is important because real sounds can be unpredictable.
Speech, percussion, claps, and other transient signals can briefly become much louder than their average level.
If recording level is adjusted so that the average signal is almost at 0 dBFS, those transient peaks may clip.
Too low versus too high
Recording level involves a balance.
If the signal is unnecessarily low, the recording may sit closer to the system's noise floor.
If the signal is too high, unexpected peaks may clip.
With modern 24-bit systems, it is generally unnecessary to record extremely close to 0 dBFS.
A clean signal with comfortable headroom is usually preferable to a hotter signal that risks clipping.
Peak and average level
A signal can have a low average level but still contain high peaks.
For example, a spoken phrase may spend much of its time at moderate level while a plosive consonant suddenly creates a much larger transient.
This is why peak meters are useful during recording.
They show the highest instantaneous levels, not merely an average.
Analog clipping versus digital clipping
Clipping can occur at different stages.
A microphone preamplifier can overload before the signal reaches the converter.
An analog circuit may saturate.
The ADC itself may clip.
A digital processing stage may exceed its expected level.
These forms of overload can sound different, but the central principle remains:
Every stage has a finite operating range.
Good gain staging keeps the signal comfortably inside that range.
Practical example
You record a short spoken phrase.
Normal peaks reach:
−14 dBFS
One louder word reaches:
−7 dBFS
This still leaves 7 dB of peak headroom.
If you increase input gain by 10 dB, that same peak would attempt to reach approximately:
+3 dBFS
The fixed digital system cannot represent that peak cleanly, so clipping would occur.
Take away
 0 dBFS represents the digital full-scale limit.
 Signals that exceed the available range can clip.
 Clipping changes waveform shape and introduces distortion.
 Headroom protects against unpredictable peaks.
 High-quality recording does not require peaks to sit near 0 dBFS.
 Gain must be managed throughout the entire signal chain.

lessons.title: Mono, Stereo and Channel Relationships
lessons.body:
A mono recording contains one audio channel.
A stereo recording contains two channels, normally called:
Left
Right
Stereo allows differences between the two channels to create a sense of spatial width and position.
If a sound is identical in both channels and played at equal levels, it is usually perceived near the centre of the stereo image.
If the sound is stronger in the left channel, it tends to move toward the left.
If different timing, level, or spectral information reaches each channel, the auditory system uses those differences to interpret spatial position and width.
Level differences
One simple stereo cue is an interchannel level difference.
Suppose a signal is:
Left:
0 dB relative level
Right:
−10 dB
The sound will generally be perceived toward the left side rather than in the centre.
This is the basis of simple stereo panning.
Timing differences
Our hearing is also sensitive to differences in arrival time between the ears.
A sound arriving slightly earlier at one ear can contribute to directional perception.
In stereo production, small timing differences between channels can create width.
However, these differences can also create problems when the channels are combined to mono.
Mono compatibility
When stereo channels are summed:
Mono = Left + Right
phase differences between them become important.
If the left and right channels contain similar signals that are nearly in phase, they reinforce.
If they contain opposing versions of the same signal, parts of the signal may cancel.
This is called a mono compatibility problem.
Bass is often kept relatively centred in many production contexts because strong low-frequency phase differences can create unstable reproduction and cancellation when summed.
This is not an absolute rule, but it is a useful design principle.
Why low bass often feels central
At low frequencies, wavelength is long relative to the size of the human head.
This reduces some of the directional cues that are strong at higher frequencies.
As a result, deep bass localization is generally less precise than localization of higher-frequency content.
Room reflections and subwoofer placement can still influence perceived location, especially when higher-frequency components or distortion are present.
Correlation concept
Stereo systems sometimes use a correlation meter to indicate how similar the two channels are.
Very roughly:
+1 indicates highly similar/in-phase content.
0 indicates weak correlation.
−1 indicates strongly opposing relationships.
A strongly negative result can be a warning that mono summing may create significant cancellation.
Practical example
Record the same voice on two channels.
In Version A, both channels are identical.
The voice sounds firmly centered.
In Version B, delay the right channel slightly.
The sound may become wider.
Now combine both versions to mono.
Version A remains largely stable.
Version B may change in tone because the delayed copy interferes with the original at different frequencies.
Take away
 Mono contains one channel; stereo normally contains left and right channels.
 Level differences can move perceived sound position.
 Timing differences can create width.
 Stereo phase relationships affect mono compatibility.
 Deep bass is generally less precisely localized than higher frequencies.
 Extremely wide low-frequency content can create cancellation problems when summed.

lessons.title: Reversing Audio: What Actually Changes?
lessons.body:
Reversing audio sounds unusual because the time order of every event is inverted.
If an original recording contains samples arranged as:
A → B → C → D → E
the reversed version becomes:
E → D → C → B → A
The individual samples are not automatically replaced with new frequency values.
Instead, their order in time is reversed.
This simple operation has surprisingly large perceptual consequences.
Forward versus reversed sound
Consider a spoken word.
Speech contains a sequence of:
 consonant attacks
 vowels
 transitions
 breaths
 decays
Our brain has learned to recognize these patterns in their normal temporal order.
When the audio is reversed, the spectral content still exists, but its evolution through time is inverted.
A sound that originally begins sharply and fades slowly may become a sound that rises gradually and stops abruptly.
This is especially obvious with percussive sounds.
Example: a clap
A normal clap contains:
Fast attack → decay
When reversed:
Rising decay tail → sudden ending
This unusual envelope makes reversed percussion easy to recognize.
What happens to frequency?
A common misconception is that reversing audio changes low frequencies into high frequencies or changes the pitch direction.
It does not.
A steady 100 Hz sine wave reversed in time is still a 100 Hz sine wave, apart from phase orientation and boundary effects.
The frequency magnitude content of a complete time-reversed signal remains fundamentally related to the original spectrum.
What changes most dramatically is:
when spectral events occur
rather than which steady frequencies exist.
Why speech becomes difficult to understand
Speech recognition depends heavily on temporal order.
The brain expects phonetic transitions to occur in familiar sequences.
For example, a consonant may lead into a vowel in a particular way.
Reversing the recording turns those transitions backward.
The resulting sound may still resemble human speech, but the timing patterns no longer correspond to normal spoken language.
Reverse-speaking experiment
This creates an interesting challenge.
Step 1:
Record yourself saying a short word or phrase.
Step 2:
Reverse the recording.
Step 3:
Listen carefully to the reversed version.
Step 4:
Try to imitate that reversed sound manually.
Step 5:
Record your imitation.
Step 6:
Reverse your second recording.
If your imitation was accurate, the final reversal may begin to resemble the original phrase.
This is difficult because you are not simply repeating normal speech.
You are attempting to reproduce:
 reversed consonant transitions
 reversed envelopes
 unusual timing
 unfamiliar articulation
 transformed breathing patterns
Comparing the recordings
A simple comparison can examine:
 duration
 waveform envelope
 spectral similarity
 timing
 peak positions
 overall level
A more advanced comparison might use correlation or feature-based audio analysis.
However, two recordings do not need to be mathematically identical for the game to be useful.
The goal is to demonstrate how strongly sound perception depends on time structure.
Waveform reversal
Suppose the original waveform contains 10 samples:
[1, 3, 5, 4, 2, −1, −3, −2, 0, 1]
Reversing it gives:
[1, 0, −2, −3, −1, 2, 4, 5, 3, 1]
The values themselves remain.
Their chronological order changes.
Reversing twice
Mathematically, reversing the exact same digital data twice returns it to its original order.
If:
R(x)
represents reversal, then:
R(R(x)) = x
But in the reverse-speaking game, the second recording is not the original digital data.
It is a new acoustic performance.
That performance includes:
 different pronunciation
 microphone variation
 room reflections
 timing errors
 level differences
 background noise
Therefore, reversing the user's imitation does not produce a perfect copy of the original recording.
The degree of similarity becomes the challenge.
Practical example
Original word:
“Sound”
The app reverses it.
You listen to the strange reversed pronunciation and try to imitate what you hear.
Your imitation is recorded and reversed again.
The final audio may sound surprisingly close to “Sound,” or it may produce a completely different result.
Repeating the experiment helps you improve at hearing temporal details that are normally ignored.
Take away
 Audio reversal changes the temporal order of samples.
 Reversal does not automatically change a steady tone's fundamental frequency.
 Envelopes and transients become temporally inverted.
 Speech becomes difficult to understand because phonetic transitions occur backward.
 Reversing the same digital recording twice restores the original sample order.
 Re-recording a reversed sound introduces new acoustic differences.
 Reverse-audio experiments demonstrate how strongly hearing depends on timing.

title: Loudness, Hearing & Sound Measurement
description: This module explains how physical sound level becomes perceived loudness, how decibels are measured, why the ear responds differently across frequency, what SPL meters actually show, and why bass can feel weak or powerful even when the measured level appears similar.

lessons.title: Sound Pressure Level and dB SPL
lessons.body:
Sound is physically carried through air as small variations in pressure.
To describe the strength of those pressure variations, acoustics commonly uses sound pressure level, abbreviated:
SPL
SPL is expressed in:
dB SPL
The decibel is not a direct unit of pressure. It expresses a ratio between the measured sound pressure and a reference pressure.
For sound in air, the standard reference pressure is:
20 µPa
or:

lessons.title: Pa
lessons.category: This value is close to the threshold of hearing for a healthy young listener around frequencies where human hearing is most sensitive.
lessons.duration: The formula for sound pressure level is:
lessons.body:
Formula
SPL = 20 log10(p / p₀)
Where:
p = measured RMS sound pressure
p₀ = reference sound pressure, 20 µPa
Suppose the measured pressure is:

lessons.title: Pa
lessons.body:
SPL = 20 log10(10,000)
SPL = 80 dB
This means the measured sound pressure is 80 dB above the reference level.
Why the scale is logarithmic
Sound pressure covers an enormous physical range.
A linear scale would produce inconvenient numbers.
The logarithmic decibel scale compresses this range into values that are easier to compare and also roughly correspond better to the way human hearing responds to changes in level.
A 10 dB increase does not mean that the physical pressure became 10 times larger.
For pressure quantities:
+20 dB = 10× pressure amplitude
+6 dB ≈ 2× pressure amplitude
This is different from acoustic intensity or electrical power, where the relationship uses 10 instead of 20 in the logarithmic formula.
Pressure versus power
For pressure:
ΔdB = 20 log10(p₂ / p₁)
For power:
ΔdB = 10 log10(P₂ / P₁)
This distinction is important.
If sound pressure doubles:
20 log10(2) ≈ +6.02 dB
If acoustic power doubles:
10 log10(2) ≈ +3.01 dB
So the phrase “double the sound” is incomplete unless we know which physical quantity is being doubled.
SPL is not the same as perceived loudness
Two sounds measured at the same dB SPL do not necessarily sound equally loud.
Human hearing sensitivity varies significantly with frequency.
For example, a very low-frequency tone may need a greater physical sound pressure level than a mid-frequency tone to produce a similar subjective impression of loudness.
Therefore:
SPL = physical measurement
while:
Loudness = perceptual response
They are related, but they are not identical.
Practical example
Imagine two tones measured at the listening position:
100 Hz = 60 dB SPL
1 kHz = 60 dB SPL
The meter reports equal physical sound pressure levels.
However, many listeners will perceive the 100 Hz tone as less loud than the 1 kHz tone at that level because human hearing is less sensitive to low frequencies, especially at lower playback levels.
Take away
 SPL measures acoustic pressure relative to a reference.
 dB SPL uses 20 µPa as the standard reference pressure in air.
 The decibel scale is logarithmic.
 Doubling pressure corresponds to approximately +6 dB.
 Doubling power corresponds to approximately +3 dB.
 Equal SPL does not guarantee equal perceived loudness.

lessons.title: Why Our Ears Hear Frequencies Differently
lessons.body:
Human hearing is not equally sensitive to every frequency.
If a 50 Hz tone, a 1 kHz tone, and a 5 kHz tone all produce the same measured SPL, they may not sound equally loud.
Our auditory system is especially sensitive through much of the mid-frequency region, where important speech information exists.
At very low frequencies, substantially more physical level may be required before the sound feels equally prominent.
This relationship also changes with listening level.
At quiet playback levels, the difference between bass sensitivity and midrange sensitivity is especially strong.
As the overall playback level rises, the perceived balance between low, middle, and high frequencies tends to become somewhat more even.
Equal-loudness contours
This behavior is commonly represented using equal-loudness contours.
Each contour connects frequencies that listeners perceive as approximately equally loud under standardized test conditions.
The horizontal axis represents:
Frequency
The vertical axis represents:
Sound Pressure Level
A contour may show that a low-frequency tone needs substantially more dB SPL than a mid-frequency tone to produce a comparable perceived loudness.
This is important because our perception does not follow a perfectly flat relationship with physical level.
Example
Suppose a listener hears a 1 kHz tone comfortably at a moderate level.
To make a 50 Hz tone seem equally loud, the 50 Hz tone may need to be reproduced at a higher SPL.
The exact difference depends on:
 overall level
 frequency
 listener
 hearing condition
 test environment
So there is no single fixed “bass compensation” value that works universally.
Why bass disappears at low volume
Imagine a music mix played loudly.
The bass feels balanced with the vocals and instruments.
Now lower the master volume significantly.
The measured level of every part of the signal decreases.
However, because hearing sensitivity changes with both frequency and level, the bass may seem to fall away faster perceptually.
The mix can now feel dominated by the midrange.
This is one reason some playback systems include loudness compensation.
A loudness-compensation curve can increase low-frequency and sometimes high-frequency energy at lower playback levels.
The objective is to compensate partly for the frequency-dependent sensitivity of human hearing.
Loudness controls are not simple bass boosts
A well-designed loudness system should ideally depend on playback level.
At low listening levels, more compensation may be useful.
At high listening levels, less compensation is required.
A fixed bass boost does not adapt to this relationship.
Individual differences
Equal-loudness data describes typical responses across groups of listeners.
Individual hearing can differ because of:
 age
 hearing damage
 ear anatomy
 previous noise exposure
 temporary hearing conditions
 individual sensitivity
So psychoacoustic curves describe general human behavior rather than guaranteeing exactly what one person will hear.
Practical example
You listen to a track at a comfortable high level and notice a deep bass line.
Reduce the volume substantially.
The bass line may seem much less prominent even though the playback system is reducing all frequencies together.
Raise the level again and the bass appears more balanced.
The signal did not necessarily change its frequency balance.
Your auditory sensitivity changed relative to the playback level.
Take away
 Human hearing sensitivity varies with frequency.
 Mid frequencies are generally heard more efficiently than very low frequencies.
 Perceived tonal balance changes with playback level.
 Bass can seem weaker when the master level is reduced.
 Equal-loudness contours describe frequencies that are perceived as similarly loud.
 Loudness compensation attempts to account for this perceptual behavior.

lessons.title: Peak, RMS and Average Level
lessons.body:
A single audio signal can have several different level measurements.
Two of the most important are:
Peak level
and:
RMS level
They describe different characteristics of the signal.
Peak level
Peak level identifies the largest instantaneous amplitude reached by the signal.
For example, a digital recording might have a maximum peak of:
−3 dBFS
This means its highest sample or reconstructed peak approaches digital full scale but remains below 0 dBFS.
Peak level is extremely important for preventing clipping.
A short transient may reach a high peak even when the rest of the signal is relatively quiet.
Examples include:
 drum hits
 claps
 consonants
 clicks
 impacts
RMS level
RMS stands for:
Root Mean Square
RMS provides a measure related to the average energy of a varying signal.
For a sequence of values:
x₁, x₂, x₃ ... xₙ
the RMS value is:
Formula
RMS = √[(x₁² + x₂² + ... + xₙ²) / N]
The values are squared, averaged, and then square-rooted.
This prevents positive and negative waveform values from cancelling each other.
Why a normal average fails
Consider a sine wave.
Over one complete cycle, the positive half and negative half are symmetric.
A simple arithmetic average may be close to:
0
But the signal clearly contains energy.
RMS produces a positive measure that better represents signal magnitude.
