Sine-wave relationship
For a sine wave with peak amplitude:
Apeak
the RMS amplitude is:
Arms = Apeak / √2
which is approximately:
Arms ≈ 0.707 × Apeak
If:
Apeak = 1
then:
Arms ≈ 0.707
In decibel terms, this difference is approximately:
−3.01 dB
So an ideal sine wave whose peak is 0 dBFS would have an RMS value around:
−3.01 dBFS
if measured using the same full-scale amplitude reference.
Different signals can share the same peak
Imagine two recordings.
Recording A:
One short impulse reaches:
−1 dBFS
but most of the recording is quiet.
Recording B:
A sustained sound remains close to:
−4 dBFS
for several seconds.
Recording A has the higher peak.
Recording B may have much greater average energy and may sound substantially louder overall.
Peak level therefore tells us very little about sustained loudness by itself.
Crest factor
The difference between peak level and RMS level is often described using crest factor.
A simplified relationship is:
Crest Factor = Peak Level − RMS Level
expressed in dB.
A highly dynamic signal may have a large crest factor.
A heavily compressed signal may have a smaller crest factor.
Example:
Peak:
−1 dBFS
RMS:
−15 dBFS
Crest factor:
14 dB
Another signal:
Peak:
−1 dBFS
RMS:
−6 dBFS
Crest factor:
5 dB
Both have the same peak level.
The second signal carries much more sustained level.
Why this matters for bass
Bass signals can consume significant headroom.
A strong low-frequency sine wave may not visually appear as spiky as a transient, but it can contain substantial sustained energy.
This places demands on:
 amplifier power
 loudspeaker excursion
 thermal capacity
 limiter systems
So peak-only monitoring does not tell the full story.
Practical example
Track A:
Peak = −1 dBFS
RMS = −17 dBFS
Track B:
Peak = −1 dBFS
RMS = −8 dBFS
Both tracks have identical maximum peaks.
Track B has far greater average signal energy and will likely feel much denser and louder.
Take away
 Peak level shows the highest instantaneous amplitude.
 RMS describes signal magnitude over time.
 Peak meters are essential for clipping prevention.
 RMS provides more information about sustained signal energy.
 Two signals can have identical peaks but very different average levels.
 Crest factor describes the relationship between peak and RMS level.
 Bass can place high sustained demands on a playback system.

lessons.title: Frequency Weighting: A, C and Z
lessons.body:
A sound level meter does not always treat every frequency equally.
Depending on the selected measurement mode, the meter may apply a frequency weighting curve before calculating the reported level.
Three commonly encountered weightings are:
A-weighting
C-weighting
Z-weighting
They serve different measurement purposes.
A-weighting
A-weighting is designed to approximate aspects of human hearing sensitivity at moderate sound levels.
It reduces the contribution of very low frequencies substantially and also changes the response at very high frequencies.
Measurements are commonly written as:
dBA
or:
dB(A)
Because low frequencies are strongly de-emphasized, an A-weighted measurement may underrepresent the physical significance of strong bass compared with a flatter measurement.
This does not make A-weighting incorrect.
It simply means the result answers a specific type of measurement question.
C-weighting
C-weighting is much flatter across a broad portion of the audible range.
It still applies some frequency shaping, but low-frequency content contributes much more strongly than it does under A-weighting.
Measurements may be written as:
dBC
or:
dB(C)
C-weighting is often useful when evaluating:
 high-level sound
 bass-heavy environments
 peak noise
 low-frequency contribution
Z-weighting
Z-weighting means approximately zero frequency weighting across the specified measurement range.
It aims to provide a substantially flatter frequency response than A- or C-weighting.
Measurements may be written as:
dBZ
or:
dB(Z)
If you want a measurement closer to the actual broadband physical SPL without perceptual weighting, Z-weighting can be useful when supported by the measurement equipment.
Why the same sound gives different numbers
Imagine a sound dominated by 50 Hz energy.
The meter might report:
80 dBA
while a C-weighted measurement could report:
92 dBC
The exact values depend on the real signal, but the principle is important.
The physical sound did not change.
The weighting filter changed.
A-weighting reduced the contribution of the low-frequency energy more strongly.
Weighting does not equal quality
There is no universally “best” weighting.
The correct weighting depends on what you are trying to evaluate.
If you are assessing environmental noise exposure according to a specific standard, that standard may define the required weighting.
If you are studying subwoofer output, a heavily bass-deemphasized curve may hide useful information.
If you are comparing full-range physical output, a flatter weighting may make more sense.
Frequency weighting versus time weighting
Do not confuse frequency weighting with time weighting.
Frequency weighting determines how different frequencies contribute.
Time weighting determines how quickly the meter responds to changing level.
These are separate settings.
Practical example
You measure music containing strong sub-bass.
First:
A-weighting: 78 dBA
Then:
C-weighting: 88 dBC
The 10 dB difference does not mean the room suddenly became louder.
It means the C-weighted measurement includes far more of the low-frequency energy.
Take away
 Sound level meters can apply frequency weighting.
 A-weighting reduces low-frequency contribution strongly.
 C-weighting retains much more bass information.
 Z-weighting is approximately flat across its specified range.
 Different weightings can produce different dB readings for the same sound.
 Choose the weighting according to the measurement purpose.

lessons.title: Distance, Level Loss and the Inverse-Square Principle
lessons.body:
As sound travels away from a source in open space, its energy spreads across an increasingly large area.
For an ideal point source radiating uniformly in free space, sound intensity follows the inverse-square law.
This means intensity is proportional to:
Formula
I ∝ 1 / r²
Where:
I = sound intensity
r = distance from the source
If distance doubles:
r → 2r
then intensity becomes:
1 / (2²) = 1/4
So doubling distance reduces intensity to one quarter.
In decibel terms:
10 log10(1/4) ≈ −6.02 dB
Therefore, under ideal free-field conditions:
Doubling distance ≈ −6 dB SPL
Example
Suppose a source produces:
90 dB SPL at 1 m
An idealized free-field prediction would be:
2 m → 84 dB SPL
4 m → 78 dB SPL
8 m → 72 dB SPL
Each doubling of distance produces approximately another 6 dB reduction.
General distance formula
The level difference between two distances can be estimated as:
ΔL = 20 log10(r₁ / r₂)
Where:
r₁ = original distance
r₂ = new distance
Suppose:
r₁ = 1 m
r₂ = 3 m
Then:
ΔL = 20 log10(1 / 3)
ΔL ≈ −9.54 dB
So the theoretical level at 3 m would be about 9.5 dB lower than at 1 m in ideal free-field conditions.
Why rooms behave differently
Real rooms are not free fields.
Walls, floors, ceilings, and objects reflect sound.
At greater distances, reflected energy may become a larger portion of what the listener hears.
This means SPL may not continue falling at exactly 6 dB per distance doubling.
At low frequencies, room modes and boundary reinforcement can dominate the result.
A listener farther away may sometimes measure more bass at a particular frequency than a listener closer to the source.
That may appear to contradict the inverse-square law, but it does not.
The inverse-square law describes an ideal propagation condition.
The room introduces additional reflected sources and interference.
Near field and far field
Very close to a loudspeaker, acoustic behavior can also differ from the simple idealized model.
Different parts of the driver or enclosure may contribute in complex ways.
At greater distances, the source may behave more like a unified radiator.
The exact transition depends on the size and design of the source and the frequency being considered.
Multiple sources
If two independent equal-level sound sources combine incoherently at a listening point, total sound power can increase by approximately:
+3 dB
If two coherent signals combine perfectly in phase with equal pressure amplitude, the increase can theoretically reach:
+6 dB
However, real loudspeakers in rooms rarely combine perfectly at every frequency and position.
Interference causes the result to vary spatially.
Practical example
A speaker measures:
88 dB SPL at 1 m
In an outdoor open environment, an approximate prediction is:
2 m ≈ 82 dB SPL
4 m ≈ 76 dB SPL
Now perform the same measurement inside a reflective room.
You may observe smaller reductions with distance because reflected sound adds energy.
At certain bass frequencies, room modes may even create local increases.
Take away
 In ideal free space, sound intensity falls with the square of distance.
 Doubling distance produces approximately a 6 dB SPL reduction for a point source.
 The distance relationship can be calculated using logarithms.
 Reflections make real rooms behave differently from ideal free space.
 Low-frequency room modes can dominate simple distance effects.
 Multiple sources can increase level, but their phase relationship matters.
